facts.text: Bethesda’s name comes from the biblical Pool of Bethesda, symbolizing a house of mercy, and was officially adopted when the post office opened in 1888.
Early settlers arrived in the 1840s by White River ferries and steamboats, establishing farms, grist mills, cotton gins, and sawmills by the late 19th century.
On February 19, 1864, Confederate forces ambushed a Union foraging party at Waugh’s Farm, killing four Union soldiers and capturing thirty‑two.
The Union Pacific Railroad ran along the White River’s southern bank just below Bethesda, linking the town to regional trade in the late 1800s.
Since 1948, the Oran McBride Stone Company has quarried limestone, sandstone, and marble near Bethesda, supplying building materials for the region.
Every summer, Bethesda hosts its annual Day Parade, a community celebration that showcases local traditions and brings residents together.
